newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak banks look to skirt new c.bank measures.
newsitem.headline: Slovak banks look to skirt new c.bank measures.

text.p: Some Slovak banks, looking to skirt new central bank forex measures, have begun a two-tier quotation system, offering foreign clients lower bid rates on deposits than domestic clients, analysts said on Monday.

The National Bank of Slovakia (NBS) set new rules at the beginning of the year for foreign exchange positions for monetary purposes -- and penalties for breaching the measures -- in an attempt to reduce the sector's rapid loan expansion.
But dealers said some banks have begun to offer discounts on depo rates to foreign clients to offset the costs of the central bank move and attract sorely-needed liquidity.

"Foreign interest in the crown is limited by sanctions the local banks must pay for breaching the measure, but it can be bridged by deducting the sanction from crown deposit bids," Emil Vitazka, a dealer with VUB credit bank, told Reuters.
"(But) even lower bids are very attractive, and we're seeing the first swaps and outrights from abroad for up to one month mainly."

The new NBS measures, aimed at reversing the trend of banks repatriating foreign assets to fund lending at home, require banks to exclude foreign exchange assets held locally from their forex position, but include crown liabilities to banks outside Slovakia.
Banks also were forced to reach a minimum ratio of foreign exchange assets and liabilities of 0.65 to start the year, rising gradually to at least 0.8 by June 30, 1997.
If banks fail to meet the required ratio, they will be fined by an increase in their minimum reserves requirements.
Bankers, however, predicted the measure may become ineffective since banks can ignore the obligation to meet the ratio, calculating losses from fines into their credit rates.
They estimate such a fine for breaching the forex position measure could lower bids by about 1.0-4.0 percent, varying from bank to bank.

"Last Friday and Monday are the days when local banks can deposit crowns for foreigners without breaking their own forex position measure -- but only for one week," said Martin Hrozany, chief dealer Slovenska Sporitelna.

Analysts said that banks most likely to offer lower bid rates are those which are experiencing liquidity problems after extending large volumes of loans and seek to cover crown shortages by foreign exchange sales to the central bank.
"Only a bank which decides to breach the measure can deposit their crowns for a longer-term," Hrozany added.

Dealers said Sporitelna, the largest liquidity supplier on the market, would not need to offer special rates, but others with a weaker foreign exchange liability position may be forced to in order to keep up a portion of their lending activities.

The NBS has said commercial banks should have enough room to adjust their activities in order to meet the required ratio. But, it warns, it still has other tools to ensure the requirements if the banks decide to ignore the measure.
The NBS reviews banks's ratio on the tenth day of each month. To allow local banks to meet the ratio, foreigners can only hold local corporate securities and state bonds as of the days of the review.

If bank fails to meet the new limit, the NBS may raise its minimum reserve requirement for three months by nine percent of a calcuation of the difference between the real and required ratio multiplied by the bank's average of forex liabilities.
The crown strengthened on Monday due to local and foreign banks purchases, settling at around 1.55 percent below its dollar/mark basket midpoint after trading at -2.0 percent early on Friday.
The overall volume of credits rose in September by some 1.3 billion crowns ($40 million), putting the total volume at 355.4 billion as of September 30 -- a 19.2 percent increase year-on-year.

Hard currency credits, which increased by 0.8 billion crowns in September, accounted for 11.3 percent of the overall volume of loans, compared with 11.1 percent at the end of August. The NBS has stated its year-end target of an increase in total credits at 7.2 percent.
($1=32.21 Slovak Crown)
